Deleted an article by yoyoman337 at -20 with three staff votes, summary deletion.

Description: SCP-5603 is 5'10 male of English decent who goes by the name of "Kevin". SCP-5603 has blue eyes, has short brown hair, appears to be between the ages of 20 to 25, and according to him is "the quiet type". SCP-5603 is also observed to be very friendly but demanding. SCP-5603's ability is to always speak truthfully. if something SCP-5603 says is not true it will become true. SCP-5603 describes his ability as "Speaking the word of truth" and "Always being right", these statements have been proven to be true. SCP-5603 is immortal and cannot physically get hurt as per his statement. SCP-5603 claims to have had many names and Kevin is the name that he has liked these past couple of years. SCP-5603 has at many times used his ability to do magic tricks as it is one of the past times he still finds enjoyable. When asked if SCP-5603 plans on escaping the foundation he said "No not now anyway but maybe another time. Besides, I find this place interesting, at least until I say otherwise. Also you're going to get me a glass of iced tea." after saying this Dr.[REDACTED] immediately sprinted out of the room and burst into the kitchen to find iced tea. after finding iced tea she poured it in a glass and sprinted back spilling most of the drink. Once Dr.[REDACTED] returned with the almost empty glass SCP-5603 took it and spoke "Guess i shoulda been more specific"

Feedback is as follows:

+ TheBlueShark
– TheBlueShark

Yeah sorry, but judging by Special Containment Procedures this is not a good SCP. And making a Humanoid SCP as your first SCP because Humanoid SCPs are really hard to get right, next time try making an Object SCP. Another thing is that you have classified this as a "Keter", Keter SCPs are SCPs that are hard to contain, this SCP is very easy to contain, so this should be classified as "Safe".

+ Spaser
– Spaser

Hello I've noticed that the formatting is very off, I recommend going to the how to write an SCP page as it has a lot of resources for formatting. It is also required that new writers get their ideas greenlighted at The Idea Critique forum before writing it. best of luck.

+ Studoku
– Studoku

In future, it's best to receive feedback before posting. The forums can help with this.

You would also have been told that this is extremely similar to a season 1 skip. On the one hand, that was a pen and paper whereas this is alive so there's room for original ideas. On the other hand, you haven't included any.

I'd shelve this concept- writing an omnipotent entity is damn-near impossible for an experienced writer. It also feels like a self-insert, Kevin.

Numerous issues

  • Spelling errors such as "decent" instead of "descent". Proofread your work and get others to do so.
  • Imperial measurements. The Foundation is an international organisation and uses the metric system. That means metres and kilograms, not feet or cubits.
  • Pronouns. SCPs almost always use it/its/itself- humanising them is dangerous
  • Lack of paragraphs
  • Description is very rambly and doesn't fit the expected tone
  • The tests add nothing new to the article. They could have been used to give insight on your SCP's personality but you decided to simply state it in the description
  • Crosslinking more popular SCPs is considered a lame way to piggyback on another article's popularity. "My SCP could beat 682" is especially overdone- it gets beaten up more often than Commander Worf.
  • The interview is poorly written and, again, adds nothing that you didn't state earlier. The doctor does not feel like a real character and seems far too easily surpised by a magic trick.
  • Allowing a dangerous SCP to freely roam the facility is always a bad idea. You've got an explanation for it but all this does is paint the Foundation as being complacent an/or woefully unimaginitive. I can think of ways of containing this guy so it's ridiculous that The Foundation can't.

Description: SCP-5735 is a small luminescent red sphere approximately 1cm in diameter. In the area one meter around SCP-5735 (the range will change by a few centimeters periodically) there is an gravitational pull to SCP-5735. If anything touches the object they will be sent to SCP-5735-1. SCP-5735-1 appears to be a flat plane of land. However this flat plane will often break up into smaller chunks of land up to 1 square kilometer in size each. These smaller chunks of land will often collide with each other causing other chunks of land to break off. Objects and people will also often be ██████████ ██████. This means that SCP-5735-1 is extremely unpredictable. The exit from SCP-5735-1 is seen as a 1 meter in diameter blue sphere, reports on physical contact with the sphere have had it described as having the consistency of hair gel. If someone steps into this blue sphere, they will be shot out of SCP-5735 at a rate of 30 miles per hour. (Injuries and broken bones are often seen in persons exiting SCP-5735-1) Note: There is only one exit from SCP-5735-1, meaning that someone can get trapped there (in theory) forever. Personnel who have returned from SCP-5735 have observed that hunger and thirst do not affect residents of the plane. Other bodily functions seem to stop, also.

No feedback present.

Description: SCP-5156 is a collection of ██ fireworks, comprised of various colors and sizes.1 These fireworks are anachronistic, dating many years before the creation of gunpowder2. Chemical examination shows no anomalous substances within the fireworks. While old, all fireworks are hypothetically functional if used.

Feedback is as follows:

+ BetterMyButter
– BetterMyButter

-1 for now. Too brief, not enough detail. Could be interesting but there's not much to go off of. Needs meat, if that makes any sense. I'd recommend adding more addenda to further explain the history of this thing.

Also, punctuation. I've fixed some of it for you.

Edit: Also, why is it that the author isn't shown at the bottom of the page? Strange.

+ LonLangLin
– LonLangLin

Decent idea, but there are quite a few things I find weird here. How does the Foundation know these fireworks are ancient? How does it know they're anomalous and warrant containment at all? these oddities, together with a few places where tone could be a bit better, lead me to unfortunately give this a -1 for now.

+ Idontworkhere
– Idontworkhere

-1 for me for two main reasons.
1: It just didn't really capture my attention. Too brief and not enough detail, like BettermyButter said. It needs to be fleshed out more.
2: This is non-anomalous. There isn't anything out of the ordinary here. If it was written better and sufficiently explained, it might barely work as a -EX.

+ Spaser
– Spaser

Chemical examination shows no anomalous substances within the fireworks

Then why is it an SCP? I like the concept you are going for but it certainly needs some fleshing out. I recommend going to Idea Critique forum for help turning this into a fully realized SCP but as it stands now it needs a lot of work.

+ General Goose
– General Goose

Like everyone above, the idea is too brief to develop it´s idea. I can see what you are going for, but the shortness + the non-anomalous nature makes it a -1 for me.

Deleted an article by Jakob17 at -11 with three staff votes, standard deletion process.

Benjamin Kondraki ran down of the hotel's fire escape. Blood was dripping from him as with each step as he tried to get away from his attackers.

The geese quietly followed the trail of blood left by their designated target. The assassins cornered him in a dark alleyway, where he raised his weapon ready to shoot. To his horror, the gun only gave a laughable click when he pulled the trigger. The geese charged towards him in a swarm ready to end him once and for all.

"It can't end like this…." Kondraki thought as he started punching the creatures that wanted him dead. Though it was a merciless fight, they were just too many - he couldn't take them all at the same time. As he threw his final punch, he slowly collapsed to the ground, allowing the vicious beasts to pierce into his flesh and end him forever. "Goddamnit," thought Benjamin Kondraki, as the life faded from his eyes.

Feedback is as follows:

+ Ellie3
– Ellie3

This tale (and the tale before) is beating a joke into the ground that wasn't really funny in the first place.

+ stormbreath
– stormbreath

This tale, and the one before it, are neither entertaining nor well-written. The more important of these is that it isn't funny, despite trying its best to be. Since it fails at the thing it is trying to do, I have to downvote. Moreover, there are numerous problems in the sentence structure, but the general tone of the writing is grating and not humorous. The dialogue is egregiously unrealistic. Take, for example, the following line:

"It's a story that Includes 507, lots of geese, and is way too long for me to tell it whilst fighting… this thing!" Bright shouted, still choking the goose. "Die, you goddamn Christmas Dinner!" he added.

This is not the dialogue of a man fighting a goose.

2. Estimated to have occurred in 9th century China.

SCP-5825 is an anomalous species of whale that will manifest whenever words or designations related to SCP-5825 are spoken. SCP-5825 resembles Orcinus orca, with the exception of all white spots on SCP-5825 can be several colors, most commonly orange but not limited to green, black, yellow, and red. SCP-5825 can also survive outside of the water for an indefinite period of time despite not having the biological capability to breathe outside of water.

Deleted at -13 and three votes.

Feedback Ported:

barredowl

+ show block
– hide block

The arbitrariness of the anomalous properties here kinda prevent me from getting invested into this piece. There's not a lot of rhyme or reason given to, say, why it can recognize its designation from five miles away, or why its designations run out after a while. Granted, this is not to say that everything about the anomaly has to be 100% explained, just that it should at least make sense or feel cohesive with the rest of the anomaly. Here, those properties just feel tacked on to artificially increase the stakes, and don't strike me as particularly interesting at that. Without anything that intrigued me narrative-wise, this unfortunately felt like a more convoluted version of SCP-5404.

I'm also not a huge fan of the ending: it's pretty expected, given how deliberately manufactured the table feels to deliver it, and it's undermined heavily by the comments afterward.

Voct

+ show block
– hide block

Interesting notion, very, very sloppy execution. Punctuation errors, spelling errors, and you're supposed to use metric.

And it's good that you kept track of where the image came from, but that enables me to immediately say the image can't be used here, because CBC doesn't release their images under Creative Commons.

Asdfaslas

+ show block
– hide block

To get a little specific: saying the words "big fish" when speaking about a fishing trip isn't the same thing as referring to an anomaly by something other than its designation. The person saying big fish was not speaking about the anomaly at all, wasn't referring to it, so why would it be described as having reacted to being improperly referred to, when they weren't referring to it at all?

Secondly, orcas breathe air, and you've said that this is a mostly normal orca who should not "the biological capability to breathe outside of water." Orcas have blowholes, they do not have gills, so there is no reason for you to say that it shouldn't be able to breathe outside of the water. That's normal orca stuff, not abnormal orca stuff. Flying is abnormal, appearing in midair is abnormal, but being able to breathe whilst above water isn't abnormal.

Author, I downvoted for the following reasons:

  • Improper Formatting: put your pictures in a correct box, so they load correctly. Your item number should only be your SCP number, no extra names. Your interview should be headed with an addenda or interview header. Your Title should be in all caps. Your interview should be spaced out more.
  • Overuse of the black box: You use it both in your description, your interview, and even in your special containment procedures when it's not really needed.
  • Lack of depth: There is very little here for me to work off of, and the core anomaly is quite boring.
  • Lack of clinical tone: There is very little professionalism here, when more should be present.

I urge you to take this idea to the idea forums, so it can get a professional look from some of the critters. The drafting process may take some time, but it will produce much better results than this.

My core issue with this is that like, the central narrative behind this, and even the concept of the book, aren't technically awful but the extremely rapid way in which the entire conflict of this is brought up and then resolved feels…shallow. It feels like this needs to do more with the conflict between the Serpents Hand and the Foundation for this to land right: I think we need to be shown why this is so dangerous first, followed by the Hand taking it, followed by some kind of…exploration of what happens next. Like, see e.g. SCP-3911 for an example of a SCP following a similar kind of plot line and how it shows what the stakes are so much better.

Alas, the days when a simple thing that does a thing could survive on the mainlist are largely behind us. The orphanage idea is decent; maybe if you threw in some interviews with the kids or something to further detail the story it would fare better. Relating the item's effects through the personal account of a distressed orphan rather than or in addition to the dry description would give it much more of an impact and a personal touch that the reader could connect with.

This item's biggest weakness, though, is that it's got sort of the same vibes as the famous and incredibly wholesome tear-jerker SCP-348, with the biggest difference being that this one eats your body heat instead of healing you. That, and the fact that it compels people to use it. In general, the modern user base frowns on objects that force people to do whatever thing triggers the anomalous effect because it feels like cheap writing. The addiction angle is interesting; I think that's plenty dangerous enough without an anomalous compulsion. After all, in the situation you described, the orphans probably wouldn't need to be compelled to snuggle with the pillow parent. One could discover its properties by accident, then the other kids would find out and they'd either share it when missing their parents or maybe fight over it, getting serious hypothermia in the process but not caring.

There are a lot of issues with this piece.

First of all, there are a variety of spelling and grammar errors that interfere with the clarity of the piece ("allowed" is not spelled "aloud"). The interview logs also have some formatting errors, with the first interview having the SCP numbers be XXX, etc. and the second interview having the D-class personnel number surrounded with asterisks and not in bold. Even if these issues are fixed, there is still a lot of work that needs to be done with the actual content of the SCP.

There are a lot of missing details in the file. Both of the SCPs are wearing "military uniforms". However, no information is offered about the country that these uniforms represent, a detail that the Foundation would definitely pay attention to in order to ascertain the origin of the anomaly. Also, I find it a little hard to believe that having the two entities simply "be together" resulted in the deaths of over two thousand people, not to mention over a hundred experienced Foundation staff. And despite all of this death, only a photograph was taken of the pair? We don't even get an explanation of how the picture was taken and who took it. Not only that but if the pair was so powerful, how were they even forced apart? Why are they even in containment if they could so easily kill thousands of people? Since the Foundation knew this pair was dangerous, why did a researcher go in alone without any security to interview an unpredictable SCP? And even after they learned it was dangerous, why did they send in a D-class personnel for the second interview? Couldn't they have managed just as easily and with less of a chance of casualties with a speaker system?

Finally, the overall tone of the piece does not work well. There is an attempt to use the clinical language typical of SCP's, but the effect is ruined by the inclusion of phrases such as "sloppily stitched" and "horrible mouth". The picture itself is confusing, especially since the date on the upper right-hand corner appears to be from some time in 1936 and the building behind it does not appear to correspond with the date (see the AC unit at the top left of the building).

This is getting a downvote from me. And unless there is a total rework of this piece, I don't think I'm going to be changing my vote.

This feels like it could be a lot more interesting than it actually is if it just had, a layer of polish and a little more care in the actual execution of it.

There's, places where the writing is kinda sloppy grammatically too1 : it might be worth running this through something like libreoffice's spelling and grammar checker or w/e to see if it can be tightened up, or finding someone willing to give it an LBL

My central problem with this is two fold: the build up to the ending isn't very interesting and the ending feels like it just kinda, comes out of nowhere.

Like, for the build-up, the issue is just, the narrative is very passive? There's various dates where new stuff is introduced that turns out to be from the satellite but there's no real sense of the foundation either struggling to find stuff out or really having any purpose here beyond just stumbling on answers. I'd like to highlight stuff like:

The initial design was nearly identical to SCP-5261, but without a Scranton reality anchor and with a less resilient alloy.

followed immediately by 'we added a Scranton reality anchor' and 'we added a more resilient alloy' as weird like, there's no reasoning given for these not being included before hand or real clarity on why the design is still being changed as recently as like, a year before the thing is launched when the project is four years long (like, the implication here is, I guess, that they spent ~3 years designing this thing and then ~1 year building it? But it's not clear why it would take them that long to design it?)

'we used a less resilient alloy' is also wild from an engineering perspective like, this satellite is gonna be made of thousands of materials so why is improving a single one such a focus? Why is 'resilience' the important thing here and not say, durability (the ability for it to resist cyclic loading)?

Past this, the implications of anomalous activity being correlated to mass extinctions is not awful but the idea that you can measure 'anomalous activity' using a single value is kinda…weird. It…just doesn't feel at all related to the foundation figuring out what this satellite is up to: like, there's no indications that this is what the satellite is measuring or indeed how the satellite is measuring it here until we're basically told it via graphs. Also what does '1' on an anomalous activity scale even mean here?

Why are there no anomalies at all, in deep space?

It's, almost like detecting things that are very far away is hard and also extremely limited by the speed of light (as in, if the earth anomalously exploded say, today, it'd take 25,000 years for the centre of the milky way to be able to see this); but if the anomalous activity was like 'this one rock floated briefly', how would you even record that?

Beyond this: if anomalies are a great filter, what does that actually mean for the Foundation? What does this mean for their aims? Why does it matter to anyone?

Footnotes
1. e.g. "under no circumstances" should be 'under any circumstances' and "SCP-5261 is a satellite orbiting at LEO" would perhaps be clearer as 'SCP-5261 is a satellite in a LEO.'
